transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Another attack on Riyadh's international airport in Saudi Arabia has left one person dead and 11 others injured.
It comes a day after a missile strike on a passenger terminal that killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300.
NPR's Ayyeb Etrawi reports Yemen's Houthi rebels claim responsibility for the first attack.
Riyadh airport has been hit at least four times over the past week, including twice over the weekend.
The deadliest attack was Saturday. The Houthis struck a passenger terminal there.
The Saudis released CCTV footage showing passengers, many of the Muslim pilgrims headed to Mecca,
standing in line when a fireball hits the passenger terminal and parts of the ceiling collapse.
Helicopters were seen flying in to medevac the wounded out.
And Saudi authorities say 13 people of various nationalities were killed, including a U.S. citizen.
NPR's Ayyeb Etrawi reporting from Dubai.
The Justice Department is investigating five major American television networks under antitrust laws
as part of a related court battle over press access to the White House.
NPR's David Falkenflick reports the move represents an escalation of tensions between the president and the news media.
CNN, Politico and MS now sued after President Trump banned their journalists from the White House over coverage that angered him.
A federal judge temporarily required the administration to restore their passes.
He says he'll decide by Tuesday evening.
In the meantime, the White House blocked CNN from taking part in the TV pool,
in which ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC shared logistical planning and costs to cover the president in his public appearances in smaller spaces.
The other networks refused to fill the pool when CNN had been blocked.
The Justice Department now says it's investigating that consultation, claiming it may constitute illegal antitrust behavior.
Media advocates say it's another attempt to intimidate the press.
David Falkenflick, NPR News.
Hurricane Simon has weakened to a Category 3 storm but continues to threaten Mexico's Pacific coast.
NPR's Ada Peralta reports from Mexico City.
The good news is that Hurricane Simon is expected to skirt the coast and will likely not directly hit the bigger cities along its path.
Still, Colima and Puerto Vallarta are reporting strong winds, heavy surf and flooding.
Mexican President Claudia Scheinbaum has ordered citizens in four different municipalities to shelter in place until the danger has passed.
Scheinbaum has also deployed the military in those areas to help with recovery.
The National Hurricane Center expects Hurricane Simon to weaken in the coming hours and then continue moving along the coast.
Simon is forecast to make landfall on Wednesday near Masatlan.
Forecasters say it will likely be a tropical storm by then.
Ada Peralta, NPR News, Mexico City.
This is NPR News in Washington.
Cleanup crews are clearing debris and restoring power across parts of the southeast hit by Hurricane Esai Eos.
About 170,000 customers in the Florida panhandle and southern Alabama are still without electricity.
The storm damaged buildings and brought down trees when it struck the Gulf Coast Friday as a Category 2 hurricane.
At least four people have died in storm-related incidents in Florida and Alabama.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis says he expects power to be restored to nearly everyone by tomorrow night.
A new study finds that younger and lower-income women who are diagnosed with breast cancer tend to see delays in care.
NPR's Yuki Noguchi reports.
Women under age 40 are not typically screened for breast cancer and may face potential biases in treatment if they have the disease because of their youth.
In a study published in the journal Cancer, investigators looked at data to identify the wait time for care among 1,000 individuals diagnosed with breast cancer enrolled in the Young Women's Breast Cancer Study.
It found 153 instances of patients, particularly those who are lower-income, facing delays of three months or more to see a clinician about their symptoms.
Younger patients were likely to see treatment delayed by two months or more.
The report says the delays may not have led to the need for more treatment but did not affect overall survival.
Yuki Noguchi, NPR News.
Pope Leo will undergo surgery this week to remove a small growth from his lung.
The Pope says doctors found the nodule during recent medical checks and detected it at an early stage.
This is NPR News.

Justice Department investigates five major TV networks under antitrust laws amid White House press access battle
Hurricane Simon weakens to Category 3 as it threatens Mexico's Pacific coast
Cleanup underway in Florida panhandle and Alabama after Hurricane Esai Eos; 170,000 still without power
Study finds younger, lower-income women with breast cancer face delays in care
Pope Leo to undergo surgery this week to remove small lung growth found in medical checks
